title: Pediatric Renal Replacement Therapy: CRRT, Peritoneal Dialysis and Hemodialysis
subject: ss-paediatric-nephrology

steps.say: Fluid overload exceeding ten to fifteen percent in critically ill children is a decisive trigger for initiating renal replacement.
steps.tx: Recognize critical clinical triggers and **Indications and fluid overload threshold (10-15%)** to initiate renal replacement therapy. In pediatric acute kidney injury, renal replacement is urgently indicated for refractory hyperkalemia (> 6.5 mEq/L), severe metabolic acidosis, symptomatic uremia, and particularly fluid overload exceeding 10-15% of baseline body weight, as fluid overload > 15-20% independently correlates with severe multiorgan failure and markedly increased pediatric ICU mortality.

vis.title: Pediatric Renal Replacement Indications
rows: Fatal cardiac arrhythmias and conduction arrest

steps.say: Extracorporeal circuit blood volume must never exceed eight to ten percent of the infant's total circulating volume.
steps.tx: Calculate hemodynamic constraints including **Circuit blood volume constraint (< 8-10%)** prior to pediatric cannulation. To prevent hypovolemic shock, circuit blood volume (combined volume of dialysis tubing lines and dialyzer filter) must not exceed 8-10% of the patient's estimated total blood volume (calculated at 80 mL/kg for infants); whenever the circuit exceeds 10% of circulating volume, the system must be primed with 5% albumin or packed red blood cells.

nodes.label: Compare Circuit Volume to Patient TBV
> 10% TBV: Mandatory blood or 5% albumin prime

steps.say: Continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration provides optimal hemodynamic stability for unstable children in shock.
steps.tx: Select appropriate modalities comparing **CRRT modalities: CVVH vs CVVHD vs CVVHDF** in the pediatric ICU. Continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH) utilizes convection to clear middle molecules, continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD) uses diffusion for small solute clearance, and continuous venovenous hemodiafiltration (CVVHDF) combines both convection and diffusion, delivering superior clearance in hemodynamically unstable children with septic shock and multiorgan failure.

vis.title: Comparison of Continuous Extracorporeal Modalities
rows: Removal of middle molecules and inflammatory mediators
Rapid clearance of small solutes like urea and ammonia
Maximal solute clearance in unstable septic shock

steps.tx: Trace the tubing in this picture as blood leaves the child, passes through the filter, and returns. This **continuous renal replacement therapy** circuit removes fluid and solute slowly around the clock, which suits small children who cannot tolerate rapid shifts. The choice among filtration, dialysis, or combined modes changes whether clearance depends mainly on convection, diffusion, or both mechanisms working together.
steps.say: Blood travels through the filter and back to the child in this circuit. Slow continuous removal suits unstable small children better than rapid intermittent dialysis.

steps.say: Regional citrate anticoagulation avoids systemic bleeding risks by chelating ionized calcium within the filter circuit.
steps.tx: Prescribe and monitor filter safety using **Regional citrate anticoagulation protocol** during pediatric continuous therapy. Regional citrate anticoagulation is the preferred method for pediatric CRRT; trisodium citrate is infused pre-filter to chelate ionized calcium (target circuit post-filter ionized calcium 0.25-0.40 mmol/L), while intravenous calcium gluconate or chloride is infused post-filter to normalize systemic ionized calcium (target 1.1-1.3 mmol/L).

steps.say: Citrate accumulation creates metabolic toxicity characterized by an elevated ratio of total to ionized calcium.
steps.tx: Monitor blood chemistry for signs of **Citrate toxicity and total-to-ionized calcium ratio** during continuous dialysis. Citrate accumulation occurs in severe hepatic failure or hypoperfusion; it is clinically identified by worsening metabolic acidosis with an elevated anion gap, refractory systemic hypocalcemia, and pathognomonic total serum calcium to ionized calcium ratio > 2.5, requiring immediate reduction or cessation of citrate infusion.

left.title: Normal Citrate Kinetics
points: Hepatic metabolism of citrate to bicarbonate
Total Ca to ionized Ca ratio < 2.5

right.title: Citrate Toxicity / Lock
points: Impaired hepatic clearance in shock or cirrhosis
Refractory hypocalcemia and widening anion gap
Total calcium to ionized calcium ratio > 2.5

steps.say: Acute peritoneal dialysis provides life-saving renal replacement in neonates and centers without vascular access machines.
steps.tx: Implement bedside technique for **Acute peritoneal dialysis catheter and fill volumes** in small pediatric patients. Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is the modality of choice in neonates, infants, and low-resource settings; using a flexible Tenckhoff or straight catheter, initial fill volumes start low at 10-20 mL/kg to assess tolerance, and are gradually titrated up to 30-40 mL/kg (or 800-1100 mL/m²) as tolerated without causing respiratory compromise.

vis.alt: Peritoneal dialysis in a child using the peritoneum for fluid and solute exchange.
vis.caption: Peritoneal dialysis: the peritoneum as the filter in children. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Turbid peritoneal effluent containing over one hundred white blood cells per microliter confirms acute bacterial peritonitis.
steps.tx: Rapidly diagnose and manage suspected **PD peritonitis criteria and empiric therapy** in children on dialysis. PD peritonitis is diagnosed by cloudy effluent dialysate, abdominal pain, and an effluent cell count > 100 WBC/mcL with >= 50% polymorphonuclear leukocytes; empiric treatment requires immediate intraperitoneal antibiotics covering gram-positive organisms with cefazolin or vancomycin and gram-negative coverage with ceftazidime or an aminoglycoside.

steps.say: Overly rapid clearance of urea during hemodialysis can cause life-threatening cerebral edema and neurological deterioration.
steps.tx: Institute rigorous precautions against **Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome prevention** during initiation of intermittent hemodialysis. Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome results from rapid solute (urea) clearance causing water movement into brain tissue; prevention requires limiting initial blood flow rate (3-5 mL/kg/min), limiting treatment duration to 2 hours, and restricting blood urea nitrogen reduction to < 30-40% on the inaugural hemodialysis run.

vis.title: Disequilibrium Syndrome Preventive Strategy
rows: Prevents abrupt drop in plasma osmolality
Prevents osmotic water shift into cerebral cells
